result:
There's something about lighthouses that won't leave me alone.

Not the romantic kind — not the postcard versions with seagulls circling and a golden sunset melting behind them. I mean the real ones. The cold, salt-eaten towers standing on rocks that every storm wants to swallow. The ones whose paint peels in long strips like dead skin. The ones nobody visits anymore because GPS made them largely ceremonial.

I keep thinking about the keepers. The last generations of people whose entire job was to be awake while the world slept, feeding a flame or polishing a lens so that strangers they would never meet could find their way past the rocks. They signed up for solitude the way other people sign up for jobs, and some of them went quietly mad, and some of them wrote the most honest journals of their lives because the only audience was the dark.

There's a lighthouse near where I grew up. Automated now, of course. But when I was nine or ten, my father drove me out there in February, and the wind was so violent I had to lean into it to keep standing. The beam swept over us, bright and indifferent, and I remember thinking: it doesn't know we're here. It shines whether anyone watches or not.

I've been trying to live like that. Not desperately, not for applause. Just keeping the light turning in case some small boat needs it.
